q-48637.name: Question 1
q-48637.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ at the point where $(\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).$
q-48637.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot (2) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is $\sqrt{2}.$

q-31241.name: Question 2
q-31241.worked_solution:
The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is given by ${f}^{′}(0).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u={x}^{2}+2x-1.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (2x+2) \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =(2x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+2x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0) & =(2\cdot 0+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡({0}^{2}+2\cdot 0-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=0$ is $2\operatorname{cos}⁡1.$

Find the slope of y=sin⁡(x2+2x−1) at x=0.

a
−sin⁡1
b
2cos⁡1

4cos⁡1
d
−2cos⁡1
e

The slope of y=f(x) at x=0 is given by f′(0).

y=sin⁡u,u=x2+2x−1.

We now apply the chain rule, and get

f′(x)=dydu⋅dudx=cos⁡u⋅(2x+2)=(2x+2)cos⁡u=(2x+2)cos⁡(x2+2x−1).

Evaluating at x=0, we find

f′(0)=(2⋅0+2)cos⁡(02+2⋅0−1)=2cos⁡(−1)=2cos⁡1

Therefore, the slope of y=f(x) at x=0 is 2cos⁡1.

q-48512.name: Question 3
q-48512.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2\pi -3x)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0).$
q-48512.worked_solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2\pi -3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(-{csc}^{2}⁡u)\cdot (-3) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -3x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =3{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =3\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =3(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =3x-\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-48639.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(2x)$ at the point $(\frac{\pi }{8},1).$
q-48639.worked_solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{cot}⁡u,\,u=2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=-{csc}^{2}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-{csc}^{2}⁡u\cdot (2) \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡(2x).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$, we find 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-2{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-2\cdot {(\sqrt{2})}^{2} \\  & =-4\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is $-4.$

Question 6
?

Find f′(x) when f(x)=3cos2⁡(x).

a
3cos⁡xsin2⁡x
b
6cos⁡xsin⁡x
c
−6sin2⁡x
d
−6cos⁡xsin⁡x
e
−3cos⁡xsin⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express

f(x)=3(cos⁡x)2.

Now, we see that f(x) can be expressed as the composite function

f=3u2,u=cos⁡x.

Differentiating, we get

dfdu=6u,dudx=−sin⁡x.

We now apply the chain rule, and get

f′(x)=dfdu⋅dudx=6u⋅(−sin⁡x)=6(cos⁡x)(−sin⁡x)=−6cos⁡xsin⁡x.
q-72159.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

q-48643.name: Question 7
q-48643.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

b
−cos⁡xcos⁡(sin⁡x)

q-72163.name: Question 8
q-72163.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot (\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the derivative of y=sin⁡(sec⁡x).

a
sec⁡xtan⁡xcos⁡(tan⁡x)
b
sec⁡xtan⁡xcos⁡(sec⁡x)
c
 sin⁡(sec⁡xtan⁡x)

sec⁡xtan⁡xsin⁡(sec⁡x)
e
cos⁡(sec⁡xtan⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express y as the composite function

y=sin⁡u,u=sec⁡x.

Differentiating gives

dydu=cos⁡u,dudx=sec⁡xtan⁡x.

We now apply the chain rule, and get

dydx=dydu⋅dudx=cos⁡u⋅(sec⁡xtan⁡x)=sec⁡xtan⁡xcos⁡(sec⁡x).

q-342445.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=\operatorname{sec}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡(u)\operatorname{tan}⁡(u)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$
